series.title: How long will you accept this risk?

scenarios.title: The OAuth token
scenarios.hook: Would you sign a blank power of attorney and hand it to a vendor you've never audited?
scenarios.escape: Obviously not. And you'd never delegate account authority like that… right?
scenarios.act: clicked “Authorize” on an OAuth consent screen
scenarios.reveal: A token is delegated authority that outlives the click. It doesn't ask for your password and it isn't stopped by your second factor — MFA guards the front door; the token is already inside.

scenarios.title: The company card
scenarios.hook: Would you give a brand-new hire an unlimited company card on day one — unsupervised, overnight?
scenarios.escape: Never. But nothing in your stack holds payment authority… right?
scenarios.act: given an agent access to a billing or payment API
scenarios.reveal: An agent with payment-API scope is a new hire with the card — minus the probation period, the working hours, and the manager. The authority is real, continuous, and exercised at machine speed.

scenarios.title: A database of customers' passwords
scenarios.hook: Would you keep a database whose contents are, in effect, your customers' passwords?
scenarios.escape: Of course not — you hash passwords. And you store nothing equivalent… right?
scenarios.act: stored customer OAuth tokens to power an integration
scenarios.reveal: A stored customer token is a working credential to that customer's systems — it doesn't need cracking, it needs copying. That's the pattern behind the reported Klue breach: not passwords lost, but delegated authority held in one place.

scenarios.title: Every email you own
scenarios.hook: Would you hand a stranger the keys to every email account you've ever registered?
scenarios.escape: You wouldn't. And you don't hand out inbox access anyway… right?
scenarios.act: given an assistant access to your inbox
scenarios.reveal: An agent with inbox access holds more than your mail. Every password reset for every account you own lands in that inbox — so the grant is, in effect, the keys to everything downstream.

scenarios.title: Your calendar
scenarios.hook: Would you let someone quietly rearrange or delete your entire calendar?
scenarios.escape: Of course not. But nothing you run can write to your calendar… right?
scenarios.act: connected an assistant with calendar write access
scenarios.reveal: Calendar write scope is one API call away from every event you have. The same permission that adds a meeting can move or remove all of them — there is no smaller unit of trust on offer.

scenarios.title: Your private messages
scenarios.hook: Would you let an app forward every private message you've ever sent to anyone it chooses?
scenarios.escape: No. But your integrations only read messages to be helpful… right?
scenarios.act: connected a tool that can read your messages
scenarios.reveal: Read access plus any outbound channel is forwarding capability. The permission doesn't distinguish “summarise my chats” from “send my chats elsewhere” — both are the same grant exercised.

scenarios.title: All your repositories
scenarios.hook: Would you let a bot rewrite or delete every one of your code repositories?
scenarios.escape: No chance. But your coding agent only touches the repo it's working on… right?
scenarios.act: authorised an agent against your account rather than one repository
scenarios.reveal: Account-scoped write access doesn't know which repo “the task” meant. Every repository the account can reach, the agent can reach — the scope is the account, not the intention.

scenarios.title: The production database
scenarios.hook: Would you give an unsupervised script write access to your production database, with no undo?
scenarios.escape: That's a firing offence. Nothing you run has prod credentials… right?
scenarios.act: given an agent a connection string to get a task done
scenarios.reveal: A connection string is not a task description. Write access granted for one query is write access for any query — and a wrong UPDATE has no confirmation dialog.

scenarios.title: Your unlocked laptop
scenarios.hook: Would you invite a stranger to sit at your unlocked laptop while you make coffee?
scenarios.escape: You lock your screen. And nothing else acts on your machine while you're away… right?
scenarios.act: run a local agent that reads content from the internet
scenarios.reveal: A local agent that reads untrusted content and then acts on your machine is a guest at the keyboard. What it reads decides what it types — and it is your session it types into.

scenarios.title: One customer reaching another
scenarios.hook: Would you let one customer's request reach into another customer's data?
scenarios.escape: That's the one line you never cross. And nothing in your product could… right?
scenarios.act: given an agent access that spans more than one tenant
scenarios.reveal: An agent whose scope spans tenants makes isolation a matter of prompt discipline instead of permission. One poisoned input, and a request from tenant A is exercising authority in tenant B.
